Engineers gave a trained robot a new hand, and it forgot how to do its job. Task success fell to almost zero. This was a simulation study, and all they did was swap the gripper.

Getting it back took no retraining. @hedra_labs matched the new gripper's reach and grasp point in the wrist camera and success returned to near 100%, which tells you how tightly the robot's skill was tied to the exact hand it trained with.

ChatGPT learned from the whole internet, and robots have nothing like that to learn from. There is no internet of robot data. Each robot and factory line produces its own video, sensor streams and simulation, way more data than text, and a general-purpose model wasn't built on any of it. So these teams have to train on their own data, and a lot of them have the hardware and the sims without a research lab to do it.

Model Factory, which just launched, bets those teams would rather rent that lab than build one. You bring a simulator, AI scientists run the training experiments while human researchers steer, and the model keeps collecting data after it ships. They say they ran it on their own stack first, where Krea 3's 2K image edits dropped from about 22 seconds to 3.6 on the same four AMD GPUs in under a week.

I'd judge a robotics team by how fast its second model shows up, since the first one goes stale the day somebody changes the hardware. Frontier labs already use models to help build their next model, and robots and factory floors are next in line for that loop.

Open-source is critical for robotics AI. It means a student, a researcher or a startup can build on years of progress and contribute something the whole community can use rather than concentrating everything in a few companies building a black-box robot. 

That’s why we’re building @huggingface into the platform for open-source robotics AI! Amazing to see the progress we've made in the six months and it's accelerating!

- Almost 100,000 public robotics datasets on https://t.co/QIPmkxCk57, up 48%
- Over 30,000 public robotics models, up 41%
- Microduck and Reachy mini, our open-source robots became the most popular robot of 2026 (probably ending the year with 50,000+ sold and 20,000+ shipped)
- We’re a founding partner of @RoboColosseum, evaluating robots across 140+ real-world scenes. Every run is published publicly on HF, including failures, so everyone can learn from what actually happens.

And @LeRobotHF got downloaded over 1M times and v0.7.0 just landed with new world action models, interactive robot control and remote GPU inference: https://t.co/Euoz11Ccc5!

Huge thanks to everyone making this happen 🤗🦾
